newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: SOCCER-VENABLES ENJOYING HIS TRIP DOWN UNDER.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-VENABLES ENJOYING HIS TRIP DOWN UNDER.

text.p: In his own cockney vernacular, Terry Venables has found himself a "nice little earner" in his new job as Australia national soccer coach.
Hired on a 19-month contract worth a reputed 200,000 pounds (US$327,000) a year, Venables has, on paper at least, one of the easiest jobs in world soccer.

If Australia qualify for next year's World Cup finals in France -- and they've already cruised through their Oceania qualifying group -- no other nation will have played fewer matches or faced such relatively weak opposition to get there.
His adopted soccer home has also proved a rich source of new playing talent for Portsmouth, the English first division club where Venables is chairman and part-owner.
There's even been time for the former England and Barcelona coach to film a television soft drink commercial for screening in Britain.
In the advert, which plays on a British perception of Australia as a soccer backwater, Venables is frustrated by his players' inability to master the rules and skills of the game.
At one point, Venables, wearing a sheepskin coat in searing Outback temperatures, shouts: "Don't punch it, kick it", and "In the goal not over it" as nervous players revert to Aussie rules football.

The chirpy Londoner has undeniably made an impact -- and generated welcome publicity for his employers -- in a country where soccer struggles for attention against the dominant codes of Australian rules, rugby league and union.
Venables has good reason to celebrate his new circumstances.

While the major European nations battle each other to qualify, Australia barely raised a sweat in winning their weak Oceania qualifying group, completing their programme with a 2-0 win against Tahiti on Thursday.
As group winners, Australia now face a play-off against New Zealand before a final qualifier against an Asian opponent later in the year.
It is a qualifying path that every national coach in Europe, not least Glenn Hoddle, Venables' successor in the England job, would relish.
In total, Australia will play only eight qualifying matches, six of them at home after Solomon Islands and Tahiti gave up home advantage, apparently for financial reasons.

In fact, if Venables has a complaint, it surrounds the lack of decent opposition. Australia scored a total of 26 goals and conceded two in their four group matches. Even Aston Villa goalkeeper Mark Bosnich got into the act with a penalty.
"Whatever draw we've got, we can't change it. We just have to attack it the best way we can," Venables said after one of those one-sided wins.
Several Australian national league clubs have found other reasons for complaint, however.
Their disquiet stems from the arrival of Portsmouth manager Terry Fenwick to sign three Australian league players -- goalkeeper Zeljko Kalac and midfielders Robbie Enes and Hamilton Thorp.
Venables provided Fenwick with videotapes of the players in action, something other clubs say revealed a conflict of interest for the national coach.
They argue that Portsmouth could benefit if Venables selects any of the trio for Australia, raising their profile and future value on the transfer market.
Venables has insisted there is no conflict between his two roles, saying: "It was Terry Fenwick who made the decision to buy these players."
It's a view shared by Soccer Australia chairman David Hill, who has defended Venables' actions, declaring that the ruling body has no objection to his outside activities with Portsmouth.

Nor does Hill have a problem with Venables' starring role in the television advert, which portrays Soccer Australia's headquarters as a ramshackle shed in the desert and was described by a spokeswoman for ad agency Saatchi and Saatchi as "an affectionate poke".
"Terry consulted us about it beforehand, and it sounded hilarious," said Hill.

Venables, who still lives in London and will be able to see his handiwork when he returns home from his latest stay, said:"It's a bit of a mickey-take on all of us -- England, Australia, and myself. It's a bit of fun and I was up for it."
